answer:
A RIC ETF can generally meet redemptions by transferring portfolio shares “in kind” to an authorized participant (AP), rather than selling them for cash. The ETF typically recognizes no gain on that transfer; it can also select low-basis lots to remove embedded gains. Those mechanics can reduce the fund’s realized gains—and thus capital-gain distributions—compared with a cash-dealing mutual fund that sells appreciated stocks to raise redemption cash. The ETF structure does not make gains disappear: the AP or its clients take the securities and their tax consequences, while remaining shareholders may still face gains when the fund sells assets. Cash redemptions, portfolio rebalancing, index changes, and other sales can still generate taxable distributions.

The benefit is not a guarantee of zero distributions or lower total tax in every year, and it does not eliminate tax on dividends or on an investor’s eventual sale of ETF shares. It depends on eligible in-kind operations, liquidity, and fund practice; ETF investors can also owe tax on gains from selling their shares.
